perspective:
As John Atcitty, the information available to me is:

- I am an Alaska Native man, a Heavy Equipment Operator, and I teach equipment operation at a community center. I have a middle-school education.
- Beverly Yan is my colleague at the community center; she teaches adult education classes and has a doctorate. I sometimes feel insecure about my education compared with hers.
- In our joint class project, I set up the equipment and told Beverly I hoped it met her expectations. I heard her say she has always admired how I handle machines, and that education isn’t just about degrees but what you do with what you know.
- After Beverly praised my machinery expertise, I felt more confident. I thanked her and suggested a new workshop combining theory and practice. I heard her say she loved the idea, called my practical skills invaluable, and believed we could create something special together.
- After a successful collaboration, I worried I might not always meet the recent high standards. I told Beverly I was worried. She said she appreciated my honesty, suggested realistic goals, and said our combined efforts—not perfection—make projects successful.
- After that talk, I believed Beverly valued my honesty and saw me as a reliable partner, which increased my sense of worth. I told her I was glad I could be open with her. She said she respects my openness, trusts my judgment completely, and wants transparency to continue.
- Encouraged by our collaborations and mutual respect, I felt ambitious. I proposed a larger community-wide event to showcase what we had achieved together. Beverly called it a fantastic idea, said it would demonstrate our impact, and agreed to start planning.
